title: Cap. VIII Arg. 6 Resp.: Augustine's just judgment refers to original demerit as adjunct, not motive
pass_a_gloss: Secondly, when Augustine affirms that in reprobation we ought to acknowledge the just judgment of God, that is not to be referred unto foresighted actual sins of individuals, but unto the common original debt. It therefore does not help those who deduce this reprobation from the foresight of final perseverance in actual sins. Further, we so concede consideration of original sin in this negative reprobation, that it was an adjunct adhering to the reprobated subject, but not that it was a moving cause of the Divine will unto this act of reprobating. It is therefore to be acknowledged that this act of negative reprobation, by which special grace is decreed to be denied to a person contaminated by original sin alone, is exercised not without justice, much less against justice. For (what we noted before) what is not owed from justice is sufficiently justly denied; but meantime it is to be held that it depends not from retributing and vindicating justice, but from the liberty of the Divine will, having mercy on whom it will, and passing by whom it will, that in this common guilt of original sin certain ones are decreed to be efficaciously freed, certain ones by negation of special grace to be left in that state.
pass_b_english: Second: when Augustine says that in reprobation we ought to acknowledge God's just judgment, that refers not to foresighted actual sins of individuals, but to the common original debt. So it does not help those who derive this reprobation from foresight of final perseverance in actual sins. We do grant original sin a place in negative reprobation — as an adjunct adhering to the reprobate subject, not as a moving cause of the divine will to that act of reprobating. Negative reprobation, whereby special grace is decreed denied to a person stained by original sin alone, is exercised not without justice, still less against it. What justice does not owe is justly denied; yet the discrimination — some efficaciously freed from this common original guilt, some left in that state by denial of special grace — depends not on retributing and vindicating justice, but on the liberty of the divine will, which has mercy on whom it will and passes by whom it will.
source_text: Secundo, quando Augustinus affirmat, in reprobatione nos debere agnoscere justum Dei judicium, non id ad praevisa actualia peccata singulorum, sed ad commune debitum originale est referendum. Non igitur juvat eos qui hanc reprobationem a praevisione finalis perseverantiae in actualibus peccatis deducunt. Porro, originalis peccati considerationem in hac reprobatione negativa ita concedimus, ut fuerit adjunctum adhaerens subjecto reprobato, non autem ut fuerit causa movens voluntatem Divinam ad hunc actum reprobandi. Agnoscendum itaque est, hunc actum reprobationis negativae, qua gratia specialis neganda decernitur personae solo peccato originali contaminatae, non sine justitia, multo minus contra justitiam, exerceri. Nam (quod ante annotavimus) satis juste negatur quod ex justitia non debetur; sed interim tenendum, non ex retribuente et vindicante justitia, sed ex libertate Divinae voluntatis, cujus vult miserentis, et quem vult praetereuntis, dependere, quod in communi hoc reatu originalis peccati quidam decernantur efficaciter liberandi, quidam per negationem gratiae specialis in illo statu relinquendi.
